newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Left hails Jospin plans, Right sees failure.
newsitem.headline: French Left hails Jospin plans, Right sees failure.

text.p: France's restive trade unions welcomed Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's cautious start to fulfilling costly campaign promises on Thursday while foes denounced his programme as an encore of failed Socialist policies of the past.

The unions, which may hold the key to Jospin's success by holding off on labour disruption which dogged his centre-right predecessors, gave cautious praise to the new prime minister's clean break with the policies of the previous government but made it clear they wanted more.

Communists, Greens and other factions in the governing leftist alliance took aim at some of Jospin's priorities, set out in the new Socialist leader's first policy speech to parliament, but pledged to support the coalition.
The right, ousted from power in a June 1 election, vowed resolute opposition.

Financial analysts said Jospin had committed himself to a long list of expensive measures, with a price tag difficult to pin down. French stocks plummeted following Jospin's speech, though the market later came off its lows.

But the analysts noted that Jospin had shown caution by putting off plans for a revision of the 1997 state budget until September and fulfilling two key campaign pledges through a compromise increase in the minimum wage and a gradual move to a 35-hour working week.
"I think that in the social domain he made advances which are not negligable. Nevertheless, I see some hazy or worrying aspects," said Marc Blondel of the powerful Force Ouvriere.

He and other unions as well as Communist deputies zeroed in on Jospin's call for a four percent increase in the minimum wage, known as the SMIC, when the Communists had called for an eight percent rise.
"Is it (a rise of) four percent that will not be followed by other steps?" asked Blondel, who also questioned why Jospin had not mentioned wage rises in other sectors.

"I regret that the rise (in the SMIC) is limited to four percent. I would have liked a bit more," said Communist floor leader Alain Bocquet, who went on however to pledge to support the coalition "in a responsible and constructive spirit".
Socialist Party floor leader Jean-Marc Ayrault also pledged support to the new government and praised the prime minister's responsible pace.
"Nothing would be more dangerous and more fallacious than an avalanche of measures and texts, a plea for 'everything right away'," he said.
Gaullist RPR floor leader Philippe Seguin pledged to work with its centrist UDF partner to become "a resolute and loyal opposition" to the leftist majority.
He also warned Jospin against using a planned audit of public finances as an excuse to go back on France's European commitments.
"The answers you propose are not convincing. It is obvious that you will not be counting on our vote," Seguin said.
UDF floor leader Francois d'Aubert, in a similar vein, wondered why Jospin had not directly addressed the fate of planned social security reforms and the privatisation of France Telecom.
"There are more question marks than answers," he grumbled.
The extreme-right National Front called Jospin's programme a continuation of the centre-right's failed plans and predicted it would quickly enable the Front to gain power.
"In fiscal policy, employment, immigration, education, He is going tio continue to apply the same old failed recipes," the Front said in a statement.
